title: Neuroinflammation: double-edged
objective: Contrast protective and damaging roles of CNS neuroinflammation.

steps.title: Help, then harm
steps.body: Acute neuroinflammation clears pathogens and debris and walls off damage — useful. But *sustained* neuroinflammation can injure neurons and is implicated in chronic and neurodegenerative disease. The same machinery protects early and harms when it won't resolve.

steps.prompt: Why is neuroinflammation described as double-edged?
options: Acute responses protect, but chronic ones can damage neurons
It is always purely protective, with no downside whatsoever
It is always purely destructive, with no benefit at all
It has no measurable effect on neurons in either direction
steps.explanation: The acute response defends the tissue; failure to resolve turns the same processes damaging — the core tension in neuroinflammation.

variants.setup: An inflammatory response in the CNS never shuts off.
options: Ongoing damage to neurons over time
variants.reveal: Unresolved neuroinflammation shifts from protective to damaging.

steps.setup: A therapy wipes out all microglial activity to stop neuroinflammation.
options: Losing the protective surveillance and debris-clearing microglia provide
Nothing would change, since microglia only ever do harm anyway
Astrocytes would simply take over every microglial function
The debris would be cleared by neighbouring neurons instead
steps.reveal: Because the response is double-edged, blunting it entirely can remove needed defense and clean-up. The goal is usually to resolve or rebalance it, not abolish it.

options: Losing the protective surveillance and the clean-up
Nothing changes, since microglia only do harm
Astrocytes would take over every microglial job
variants.explanation: Microglia also protect; removing them entirely loses that benefit.
